title: One of Ontario's most haunted landmarks is a historic site that has a terrifying new blackout maze
excerpt: Fort Fright is running on select nights through Oct. 31.
content:
Ontario’s Fort Henry National Historic Site is a 19th-century landmark with a dark past, having once served as a First World War internment camp.

The site’s tragic history has sparked long-standing ghost stories — so much so that it was featured on an episode of “Ghost Hunters.”

Located at 1 Fort Henry Dr. in Kingston, the site embraces its eerie lore each fall by hosting Fort Fright, running on select nights through Oct. 31.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Set within the fort’s towering limestone walls, this year’s open-air experience features a terrifying new twist: a blackout maze where visitors navigate blindfolded, guided only by a handrail.

Where monsters and mysteries come to life

Dubbed Canada’s most haunted location by “Ghost Hunters,” Fort Henry has long been a hot spot for paranormal reports. According to Glen Shackleton, the docent featured in the TV episode, both staff and visitors have witnessed unexplained phenomena over the years.

Daring guests can test those rumours for themselves. Fort Fright leans into the fortress’s spine-chilling history by blending its dramatic military architecture with immersive scares.

The debut of The Following offers the ultimate test of courage. This age 16-plus attraction forces blindfolded participants to rely entirely on their non-visual senses to navigate a mysterious path. Those who complete the trail are met by an enigmatic leader and “initiated” into a secret society.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Throughout the rest of the site, nightmares come alive with more live actors roaming the grounds than ever before, updated lighting, theatrical effects, new props, movie-quality animatronics, dark tunnels, and claustrophobic pathways.

The scares extend into the Dry Ditch and the Monster Hunt archery range, featuring frightening target challenges. Additional Halloween entertainment includes tarot readings, coffin rides, carnival games, and themed food and drinks.

For an even darker adventure, Dark Night Thursdays strip away the ambient lighting, leaving guests with nothing but a flashlight to explore the shadows. Admission for Dark Night Thursdays is $35, while general admission ranges from $25 (Oct. 8—11) to $30 (Oct. 15—18 and Oct. 22—31).

The history of Fort Henry National Historic Site

Built between 1832 and 1837 to replace a War of 1812 fortification, Fort Henry was designed to protect the naval dockyard at Point Frederick, the gateway to the Rideau Canal and the city of Kingston. It served as a critical hub along the vital trade route connecting Montreal, Ottawa, and points west.

After falling into disrepair following its use as a First World War internment camp, the fort underwent extensive restoration from 1936 to 1938 as a joint federal-provincial project. It reopened as a museum honouring the British soldiers who once served there. During the Second World War, the site was repurposed once again as a prisoner of war camp before reopening in 1948.

More spooky things to do in Kingston

Can’t get enough of Kingston’s spooky history?

Book a Ghost and Mystery Trolley Tour that kicks off at the Kingston Visitor Information Centre (209 Ontario St). Running until Nov. 1, the 90-minute tour rides past eerie landmarks such as the Kingston Penitentiary and the Rockwood Asylum, where some claim that ghosts appear.

Located at 560 King St. W., Canada’s most famous maximum-security prison, The Kingston Penitentiary, offers guided historical tours through Oct. 31. Walk through more than 180 years of Canadian penal history, step inside real cellblocks, and admire the facility’s incredible 19th-century masonry.
